title: Chapter 10. How we arrived at a society of people living alone

blocks.text: The previous chapter left a window and a shore: travelling in the virtual, and not forgetting the door. This one asks how so many of us have come to be alone, even when the house is full of screens and parcels. Pedro puts it as a history, not as a fate: “How we arrived at a society of people living alone.” Neighbours do not know one another. Before, there was talk of a world that was too full. Young people could not buy a house, marry or have children. And then came houses and living wages designed for a person on their own. That sequence must be told with real figures, and what can be measured must be distinguished from a reading — Pedro's — of what those figures mean.

blocks.text: Living alone is not, in itself, a misfortune. Some choose it. Some are widowed, some become independent with pleasure, some are well in their silence. This chapter does not point at those people. It points at a way of society in which not knowing one another becomes a custom, and in which making a life in common becomes, for many, a luxury that cannot be reached.

blocks.text: Begin with what is seen on the landing. In many buildings, neighbours barely greet one another. They share the lift and not the name. No survey is needed to recognise that scene, which belongs to the city and also to the village when the village has become a dormitory. Loneliness is not always felt as loneliness. Sometimes it is felt as haste, or as politeness, or as not wanting to disturb. The result is the same: people live next door and do not live with one another.

blocks.text: The figures, in Spain, show a change in the household, which is not the same as a change of soul, but goes with it. According to the National Statistics Institute (INE), the share of one-person households in all households was 29.1 per cent in 2024 and remained 29.1 in 2025, out of a total of more than nineteen million households. Almost three in ten households, then, are of a single person. Eurostat, using another method, puts Spain at 28.2 per cent in 2024 and 28.3 in 2025, and the European Union, in 2024, at around 35.4 per cent of one-person households. The European figure warns that this is not a local whim. Some of those households are older people, often women who have outlived a partner: ageing counts, and it should not be forgotten. Another part answers to different paths: separation, choice, or an adult life no longer organised as a couple. The figure does not say, by itself, that “everyone is alone.” It says that the household of one has become an ordinary way of living.

blocks.text: At the same time, many young people do not even reach that house. According to Eurostat, in 2025 the average age at which young people left the parental home in Spain was 30.2 years, the same as in Italy, against 26.3 years in the European Union as a whole. In 2024, the Spanish figure had been 30.0 years, against 26.2 in the EU. These are among the highest values in Europe, together with countries such as Croatia, Greece or Slovakia. Staying in the parents' home is not, in every culture, a failure; in the Mediterranean there has always been more prolonged living together. But when that living together is prolonged because a rent or a deposit cannot be paid, and a marriage or a child cannot be glimpsed, it ceases to be only a custom and becomes a jam.

blocks.text: The Youth Council of Spain's Emancipation Observatory, which is not the INE but measures this matter with care, placed, in the second half of 2024, the emancipation rate of the population aged 16 to 29 at 15.2 per cent, the lowest figure for a second half-year since at least 2006. Fewer young people, then, living away from the family home, even though work, on some indicators, was not going worse. The house, the price of housing, insecurity, make a wall. Without a home of one's own, marrying and having children are postponed, or given up. The United Nations, in its World Population Prospects 2024, includes Spain among the countries of “ultra-low” fertility, below 1.4 children per woman. It is not the only one. It is, yes, a portrait consistent with what Pedro sums up in his own way: young people could not buy a house, marry or have children.

blocks.text: And overpopulation? Here one must be honest, because the word has often been used as a cry, not as a measure. According to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024, the world had some 8.2 billion inhabitants in 2024 and, in the medium variant, would go on growing to a peak of about 10.3 billion towards the mid-2080s, then fall a little towards the end of the century. World population passed 8 billion in November 2022. At the same time, women have, on average, one child fewer than around 1990: world fertility stood at 2.25 children per woman, and two thirds of the population already lived in a country or area with fertility below 2.1, the approximate replacement level. Almost a fifth of countries, among them Spain, had ultra-low fertility.

blocks.text: The twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first filled with alarms about a planet that was too full. There were reasons to speak of limits: water, land, the climate, the sharing out. But the alarm of overpopulation lived, in Europe and in Spain, beside another reality: ever fewer children, smaller households, young people who did not leave home. It is not that the world “was full” and that therefore, here, people stopped making a household. It is that a discourse of multitude and a life of domestic scarcity — scarcity of housing, of stability, of a foreseeable future — took each other by the hand. People looked at a map of the world with billions on it and, on the landing, did not know the neighbour. They feared we were too many and, at the same time, it was made hard to be two, or three, in a house.

blocks.text: Then, Pedro says, came the houses and the living wages designed for a person on their own. This part is, in large measure, his reading of what the market and the institutions went on doing with that difficulty. At the time these lines are written, there is no universal “living wage,” under that name, designed by law for those who live alone. There is, and it can be seen, a habitat that has gradually adapted itself to the household of one: small flats, advertisements for studios, rents calculated for a single wage, benefits and allowances often processed for a one-person household, an industry of living alone that runs from the supper portion to the piece of furniture that expects no company. When starting a family became so expensive, society, instead of opening a path to life in common, went on making solitary life habitable — and sometimes profitable. The wage, if it stretches, stretches for one. The house, if it is found, is for one. The neighbour, the other side of the wall, is also one, and has no name.

blocks.text: That is the arrival at a society of people living alone. Not from one day to the next, and not because of a villain. Because of a sum: not knowing one another on the landing; a world that grew in number while, here, the house shrank; young people held back in the room of adolescence by the price of a flat; and, afterwards, a landscape of houses and of incomes cut to the measure of solitude, as if the normal thing were to have no one on the other side of the table.

blocks.text: Chapter 9 warned that the virtual can ease and also enclose. This chapter adds that the enclosure began before the headset: it began when the landing fell silent and the house of one became the horizon. A society that imagines coupons, machines and an abundance without rich or poor will also have to imagine how one comes to know the neighbour again, how a household can be formed if it is wished, and how a person's wage or coupon does not become the only architecture of life. Being alone can be a choice. A society of people living alone, when it is no longer chosen, is a forgetting. This book names it so that it will not be taken as natural.

blocks.text: A last nuance, so as not to make solitude a stigma. A society of people living alone is not cured by forcing anyone to share a flat or to form a couple. It is cured, if it is cured, by taking down the walls that prevent a choice: the price of housing, the insecurity that delays a child, the landing where people no longer say hello, the wage or the advertisement that only imagines a person on their own. That each may be alone if they wish, and accompanied if they wish, and that the neighbour may have a name again. That, more than a programme, is a measure of civilisation. The rest of this book — the machines, the coupons, equality, the virtual window — should also serve that. If not, we shall have solved bread and left the table empty.
